ubo_and_aml_profiling.statutory_law_governance: Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism (AML/CFT) Act 2009 (Public Act 2009 No. 35), sections 4, 10-14, 31-40, 53, 58-60; Companies Act 1993 (Public Act 1993 No. 105), sections 15-22, 99-100, 188-203; AML/CFT (Definitions) Regulations 2011 (SR 2011/115); Tax Administration Act 1994 and the Companies (Beneficial Ownership Information) Amendment Act 2023, to the extent in force at the time of pre-incorporation screening. New Zealand does not maintain a public UBO register; beneficial-owner information is obtained through mandatory AML/CFT customer due diligence and retained privately by reporting entities, with government access through supervisory and law-enforcement gateways.

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Registrar of Companies, New Zealand Companies Office, Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: Hague Apostille member state: issue original certificate, then New Zealand Department of Internal Affairs (DIA) appends an Apostille. Non-Hague state: issue original certificate, DIA authenticates the certificate, then the destination-state embassy or high commission in Wellington performs consular legalization. The two paths are mutually exclusive; never chain Apostille with consular legalization.

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.document_name: Certificate of Good Standing (Certificate of Compliance)
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Registrar of Companies, New Zealand Companies Office, Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: Hague Apostille member state: obtain the certificate and have DIA attach an Apostille. Non-Hague state: obtain the certificate, authenticate it with DIA, then present it to the destination-state consular authority for consular legalization. Use only one path based on the destination state's membership in the Hague Apostille Convention 1961.

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.document_name: Board Resolution appointing local representative and granting Power of Attorney
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Board of Directors of NZ_LTD, signed in the presence of a New Zealand notary public
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: Sign the resolution before a New Zealand notary public; notarization is completed in New Zealand. For Hague member states, the notarized resolution is submitted to DIA for an Apostille. For non-Hague states, the notarized resolution is certified by DIA and then legalized by the destination state's consulate or embassy in New Zealand.

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.document_name: Articles of Association (Certified Copy of the Company Constitution)
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: NZ_LTD filed with, and certified by, the New Zealand Companies Office
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: Obtain a certified copy from the Companies Office, have the certified copy acknowledged by a New Zealand notary, then either apply to DIA for an Apostille (Hague member) or have DIA authenticate it and the destination consulate legalize it (non-Hague member). Hague Apostille and consular legalization are independent and never combined.

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Qualifying New Zealand registered bank where the corporate account is established
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: The bank officer signs and seals the reference letter; a New Zealand notary certifies the officer's signature and authority. For Hague member states, DIA appends an Apostille. For non-Hague states, DIA authenticates the notarial certificate and the destination-state consulate performs consular legalization. Use only the applicable authentication route.

ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: The screening protocol requires all individuals holding 25 percent or more controlling interest, each director, every natural-person beneficial owner, and each proposed signatory to be checked continuously against the New Zealand Police Financial Intelligence Unit watch-list, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List, the consolidated United Nations Security Council sanctions lists, and the UK HM Treasury consolidated financial sanctions list. Politically Exposed Persons (PEP) status must be determined by an integrated risk engine covering foreign and domestic PEPs, immediate family members, and known close associates. Sanctions screening must run at the initial client-onboarding stage, at each transaction, and daily thereafter during the pre-incorporation period. Any sanctions match or adverse media trigger requires immediate filing of a suspicious transaction report under the AML/CFT Act 2009 and suspension of the engagement until clearance from the Financial Intelligence Unit or the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: New Zealand Companies Office online name reservation and search portal (NZ Companies Register, https://www.companiesoffice.govt.nz/companies/) operated by the Registrar of Companies under the Companies Act 1993
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: Company names must be registered in English or a Latin-alphabet form; non-Latin scripts, ideographs, and untransliterated foreign characters are not accepted for the primary registered name. The Registrar applies a four-tier naming convention: (1) identical name match, (2) near-identical variation differing only by punctuation, suffix, or legal element, (3) phonetically or visually indistinguishable name, and (4) translated or equivalent-meaning name likely to mislead. A director's statutory declaration explaining meaning, pronunciation, and transliteration must accompany any non-standard name.

stage_1.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: If the Registrar rejects a reserved name, the applicant receives a written decision identifying the statutory ground under section 15 or section 22 of the Companies Act 1993. The applicant may file a reconsideration application with the New Zealand Companies Office within 20 working days of the rejection, using the prescribed form and paying the applicable administrative fee. The application must include a statutory declaration, evidence of distinctiveness or secondary recognition, and any prior written approval from the relevant ministerial authority for a sensitive token. If the Registrar upholds the rejection, the applicant may seek judicial review in the High Court of New Zealand and may also file a new reservation using a distinctly different name during the appeal period.

incorporation_legal_framework.governing_statute_and_sections: Companies Act 1993 (Public Act 1993 No 105), as amended, including sections 10-16 (formation and commencement), section 31 (constitution), sections 124-126 (allotment and issue of shares), sections 151-158 (directors and appointment of officers), and sections 189-204 (registered office, records and register maintenance)
incorporation_legal_framework.competent_registry_authority: Registrar of Companies / Companies Office, Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE), New Zealand
incorporation_legal_framework.statutory_filing_instrument: Application for Registration of a Company filed through the New Zealand Companies Register online filing platform
incorporation_legal_framework.minimum_paid_up_capital_rule: None. New Zealand imposes no minimum issued or paid-up capital for a limited company, and there is no requirement for authorized share capital, par value, or a blocked escrow account prior to incorporation. Shares may be issued at any consideration approved by the Board of Directors, and subscriber funds may be placed in an ordinary corporate operating account. The only statutory filing cost is the Companies Office incorporation fee, plus optional fees for certified copies or special resolution filings if a custom constitution is adopted.
incorporation_legal_framework.pro_forma_first_board_resolution_en:
RESOLUTIONS OF THE FIRST BOARD OF DIRECTORS OF [COMPANY NAME] LIMITED (the Company) adopted on [Date] in accordance with the Companies Act 1993 (New Zealand). The Chairman confirmed that a quorum was duly present and that all notices required by the Companies Act and the Constitution had been waived or given. After deliberation, the Board unanimously passed the following resolutions:

1. SHARE CAPITAL SUBSCRIPTION AND ALLOTMENT. RESOLVED that the Board accept subscriptions from the subscribers named in the register of members; that the Company allot [number] ordinary shares to each subscriber at the issue price determined by the Board; that consideration be received in cash, property or services as approved by the Board; that the Register of Members and Register of Shares be opened; and that share certificates be issued under the hands of two Directors. RESOLVED FURTHER that all funds subscribed be credited fully and that no share shall be issued at a discount.

2. REGISTERED OFFICE ADOPTION. RESOLVED that the registered office of the Company be established at [Physical Address], New Zealand, and that this address be filed with the Registrar of Companies as the registered office and address for service. RESOLVED FURTHER that no change to the registered office take effect except by resolution of the Board and notification to the Registrar in accordance with sections 201 to 203 of the Companies Act.

3. BANKING AUTHORIZATION. RESOLVED that [Name of Bank] be appointed as the principal banker of the Company; that the Bank be directed to open a business current account in the name of the Company; that the account mandate require the signature of two Directors, or one Director together with the Corporate Secretary; and that electronic banking authorizations, direct debits, wire transfers and payment covenants be executed by the same signatories. RESOLVED FURTHER that the Directors are authorized to negotiate banking terms and provide indemnities required by the Bank.

4. APPOINTMENT OF STATUTORY OFFICERS. RESOLVED that [Name of Director A] and [Name of Director B] be and are hereby appointed as the first Directors of the Company; that [Name of Director A] be appointed Managing Director; that [Name of Officer] be appointed Corporate Secretary; and that an independent accountant be engaged to maintain accounting records. RESOLVED FURTHER that the Directors confirm that at least one Director will ordinarily reside in New Zealand as required by section 151 of the Companies Act.

5. GOVERNANCE AND CONTINUING AUTHORITY. RESOLVED that the Constitution attached to the incorporation application is adopted; that the Company adopts a fiscal year ending on 31 March; that the Directors and the Corporate Secretary be and are hereby authorized to execute all applications, notices, tax registrations, bank mandates and contracts necessary to implement the foregoing resolutions. RESOLVED FURTHER that these resolutions remain in full force and effect until amended or revoked by a later Board resolution.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Name availability review and incorporation application filing
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Companies Office - New Zealand Companies Register online filing portal (MBIE)
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Conduct a prior name availability search on the New Zealand Companies Register. If the proposed name is indistinguishable from an existing name or contains a prohibited word, choose a fresh name. Sign in to the Companies Office online filing exchange and select the incorporation of a limited liability company. Complete the application online by entering the company name, registered office physical address, address for service, director appointments, share structure and intended allotments. Attach the signed consent-to-act form for each director. Decide whether to adopt the default constitution or file a custom constitution. Pay the prescribed government fee by debit or credit card. Submit after integrity checks; the Companies Office will process the application and issue a certificate if all statutory criteria are satisfied.
required_dossiers: Proposed company legal name and name availability search confirmation
Registered office physical address and address for service in New Zealand
Full legal name, date of birth, residential address and service address for each proposed director
Signed consent to act as director for each director
Custom constitution (if the default constitution under Schedule 3 of the Companies Act 1993 is not adopted)
Share allocation and intended issued capital schedule
Payment instrument for the prescribed filing fee
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the name is refused as indistinguishably similar, offensive or prohibited, select an alternative name and resubmit the application. If the Companies Office issues a query on a missing or deficient field, file an amendment through the same online portal within 10 working days of receipt. A rejected application may be cured by addressing the stated objection and resubmitting; if the rejection arises from identity verification, provide certified identity documents with the Director's New Zealand physical address.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Obtain Certificate of Incorporation and New Zealand Business Number
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Registrar of Companies / Companies Office automatic statutory issuance
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Upon acceptance of the incorporation application, the Registrar of Companies automatically registers the company, allocates a unique company number and New Zealand Business Number, and issues a Certificate of Incorporation under section 13 of the Companies Act 1993. Download the certificate and verify the exact legal name, incorporation date, entity type and registered office details. Retain the certificate as conclusive evidence of registration. Open the statutory registers for directors and members using the Companies Office electronic register or an internal ledger. If a custom constitution was filed, confirm that a sealed copy is held at the registered office. From the date of incorporation, the company has full capacity to hold property, enter contracts and exercise all powers of a natural person, subject to the Companies Act and its constitution.
required_dossiers: Approved online incorporation application acknowledgment
Director consent forms
Attested custom constitution, if filed
Certificate of Incorporation PDF issued by the Companies Office
New Zealand Business Number allocation confirmation
Notification of allotment and share issuance entries
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the Certificate of Incorporation contains a typographical or administrative error, file a correction request with the Companies Office supported by a statutory declaration stating the correct particulars. If the company is erroneously registered because of false information or mistake, apply to the Registrar for cancellation and, where necessary, seek an order from the High Court under the rectification provisions of the Companies Act 1993.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Tax registration and Inland Revenue account setup
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Inland Revenue, New Zealand - myIR business gateway
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Following incorporation, verify in the Inland Revenue myIR business portal whether an IRD number has been automatically allocated to the company as a result of Companies Office data sharing. If no IRD number appears, complete the non-individual entity registration process online. Register for GST using the GST101 electronic filing if the company expects taxable supplies to exceed NZD 60,000 in any 12-month period, or immediately if voluntary GST registration is strategically beneficial for recovering input tax on cloud infrastructure, payment processing and software development costs. Confirm the company income tax status as a standard New Zealand company subject to the company tax rate. For a no-code website builder using Stripe and Paddle, determine the applicable export-of-services GST outcome for non-resident customers and the correct marketplace collection treatment to avoid double withholding or double reporting.
required_dossiers: Certificate of Incorporation
New Zealand Business Number
Proposed IRD myIR registration details
Directors' passport or prescribed New Zealand identity documents
Corporate bank account confirmation, if available
GST101 form or online GST registration
Projected taxable turnover and export revenue schedule
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the IRD number is not populated or the tax registration is queried, supply the company incorporation certificate and directors' identity documents in myIR to complete the non-individual validation. If Inland Revenue raises a residence or trading status objection, provide a tax agent engagement letter and an explanation of the software-as-a-service revenue model, including pricing, delivery, and customer jurisdiction, within 20 working days.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Corporate banking, share capital funding and AML/CFT onboarding
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Licensed New Zealand trading bank or licensed non-bank deposit taker, acting with the Board of Directors
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Execute the first board resolution approving the banking mandate and account signatories. Present the completed corporate banking package to the selected bank or licensed deposit taker. The package must include the Certificate of Incorporation, New Zealand Business Number, IRD number, constitution, board resolution authorizing account opening, and certified passports or proof-of-address documents for every director. Complete the bank's customer due diligence and Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism forms. Because the company operates a no-code website building platform and receives subscription payments through Stripe and Paddle, the bank may require an explanation of expected transaction volumes, customer jurisdictions and source of funds. Fund the corporate account with the share subscription monies, allot the shares to the subscribers, and record the allotment in the share register. No government escrow or blocked capital account is required because New Zealand has no minimum paid-up capital rule.
required_dossiers: Certificate of Incorporation
New Zealand Business Number and IRD number confirmation
Board resolution approving the banking mandate and signatories
Constitution (default or custom)
Certified passport or birth certificate of each Director
Personal residential address proof for each Director
AML/CFT source of funds declaration
Shareholder subscription agreement and share allotment record
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the bank suspends onboarding for KYC or AML/CFT reasons, provide the requested source-of-funds evidence, corporate organogram and relevant payment processor statements from Stripe and Paddle until the bank's compliance team clears the file. If the bank declines the relationship, escalate to the bank's relationship manager or apply to another licensed New Zealand bank with a more streamlined digital-client onboarding process.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Statutory registers, financial reporting calendar and digital business compliance
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Directors, Companies Office, Inland Revenue and qualified external accountant
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Establish the company's ongoing corporate governance infrastructure by opening and maintaining statutory registers for directors, shareholders, share allotments and charges, either on the Companies Office electronic register or in a secure paper ledger at the registered office. Calendar the annual return filing with the Companies Office, income tax filing with Inland Revenue, and financial statement preparation according to the company's balance date. For a no-code site builder, adopt software-as-a-service terms of use, privacy notices compliant with the Privacy Act 2020, and a record of processing for customer data collected through Stripe and Paddle. If the company will become an intermediary or financial service provider, perform an AML/CTF risk assessment. Engage a New Zealand chartered accountant as tax agent and appoint any required external auditor if the company crosses financial reporting thresholds. The statutory compliance calendar should also include director change notifications and registered office change filings.
required_dossiers: Certificate of Incorporation
New Zealand Business Number and IRD number
Register of directors, members and share allotments
Signed director consent forms and statutory officer appointments
First Board minutes and resolutions
Approved constitution
Stripe and Paddle merchant account agreements
Software platform terms of service and privacy policy templates
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If an annual return or tax filing is missed, file immediately after discovering the omission and pay any late penalty to the appropriate agency. If the Companies Office or Inland Revenue issues a compliance notice, respond within the stated period with the corrected filing and an explanation of administrative oversight. For disputed penalties, apply for remission under the applicable revenue legislation or engage the external accountant to represent the company.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.competent_industrial_authority: Not Applicable - ISIC 6201 covers computer programming activities and software publishing for a no-code website builder; no physical manufacturing, chemical, assembly or warehousing operation is established under ISIC 1xxx, 2xxx, 3xxx, 4xxx or 52xx.
industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.operating_license_title: Not Applicable - no statutory industrial or occupational operating license is required for pure digital software publishing and no-code website application building in New Zealand.

environmental_impact_assessment_eia.agency_name: Not Applicable - no New Zealand Environmental Protection Authority approval or resource consent under the Resource Management Act 1991 is required for a non-physical digital service.
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.classification_tier: Exempt / Not Applicable - the activity generates no physical installation, no point-source discharges, no land development, and no chemical or industrial process subject to environmental assessment.
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.discharge_and_emissions_standards: Nil - zero wastewater discharge, zero volatile organic compound emissions, zero hazardous waste streams, and no discharge consent needed under regional council rules for an office-based software platform.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.civil_defense_and_occupational_clearance: Not Applicable - no Civil Defense fire safety certification, structural load inspection or industrial workplace approval is required because the registered activity is purely digital. General office-premises obligations under the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015 still apply, including first aid, electrical safety and a documented workplace safety policy, but no special civil defense permit is triggered.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Inland Revenue Department (IRD / Te Tari Taake) of New Zealand; online taxpayer portal is myIR, accessible through ird.govt.nz, with company incorporation and business registration also anchored in the New Zealand Companies Office and the New Zealand Business Number (NZBN) regime.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: Step 1: Incorporate the New Zealand limited company (NZ LTD) under the Companies Act 1993 through the New Zealand Companies Office online register; the company automatically obtains an NZBN and an IRD number (tax file number). Step 2: For a non-resident foreign entity not incorporated in New Zealand, apply through myIR for a New Zealand IRD number using the non-resident tax registration process. This requires proof of the foreign entity's legal existence (certificate of incorporation or equivalent), the entity's registered business address, full legal name and date of birth for each natural-person director or principal, a New Zealand address for service or an electronic equivalent accepted by IRD, and a declaration of intended New Zealand business activity and estimated turnover. Step 3: If the entity is or will be carrying on taxable activity in New Zealand or supplies remote services to New Zealand residents above the statutory threshold, complete GST registration through the same myIR profile by disclosing the actual or expected 12-month taxable supply value. Step 4: IRD activates the GST registration under the same IRD number; no separate GST number is issued. Step 5: Maintain the Companies Office and myIR records as the source of truth and update any changes in directors, shareholders, address for service, or business activity within statutory timeframes.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.default_entity_tax_classification: Entity_Level_Taxation (a New Zealand-resident limited company is taxed at the entity level on worldwide income; a non-resident foreign company is within Territorial_Scope for New Zealand-sourced income only; no general pass-through eligibility and no Tax_Exempt_Zone status for an ordinary NZ LTD).
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: No US-style check-the-box election exists in New Zealand. Eligible closely-held New Zealand-resident limited companies may elect Look-Through Company (LTC) status under the Income Tax Act 2007 subpart HB, but that election is available only where all shareholders are natural persons satisfying New Zealand residency conditions. New Zealand also applies hybrid mismatch rules from the Taxation (Neutralising Base Erosion and Profit Shifting) Act 2018, which restrict double-non-taxation outcomes for hybrid financial instruments and hybrid entities; no generic pass-through election is available for a non-resident shareholder.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: Goods and Services Tax (GST) under the Goods and Services Tax Act 1985
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: NZD 60,000 of taxable supplies in any 12-month rolling period triggers mandatory GST registration; non-resident suppliers of remote services (including digital and low-code / software-as-a-service offerings) must register if they supply more than NZD 60,000 of remote services to New Zealand residents in a 12-month period. Registration is also mandatory where the person intends to make taxable supplies exceeding the threshold in the next 12 months.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: New Zealand does not impose a mandatory real-time fiscal clearance, continuous transaction control, government API authorization, or anti-fraud digital stamping regime. E-invoicing is voluntary and operates through the New Zealand PEPPOL network. Inland Revenue accepts electronic records and tax invoices, provided the invoice contains the statutory content prescribed by the Goods and Services Tax Act 1985 and Tax Administration Act 1994: supplier legal name and IRD number, issue date, description of supply, tax-exclusive amount, and either the GST amount or a clear statement that the price includes GST, the total payable, and the required tax-invoice wording where applicable. There is no pre-clearance requirement before issuing a GST invoice.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: Export zero-rating at 0% GST is available under the Goods and Services Tax Act 1985 when the supplier makes a supply of goods that are physically exported from New Zealand, either by the supplier or by the overseas recipient, and the goods are removed from New Zealand within the statutory timeframe; or when services are supplied to a non-resident person located outside New Zealand and the services are not directly connected to New Zealand land, not supplied in respect of tangible goods situated in New Zealand at the time of supply, and not services supplied to a person in New Zealand. For the no-code website builder and software-as-a-service scope, qualifying digital services supplied to an overseas non-resident are eligible for zero-rating if the supplier holds two or more consistent, non-conflicting pieces of business evidence proving the recipient is outside New Zealand, such as the recipient's business address, IP country, bank account country, telephone country code, billing address, or foreign tax identification number. Zero-rating is only substantiated if the exporter keeps complete records showing the true destination of the goods or the true non-resident identity of the digital-service recipient; a bare assertion of foreign sale is insufficient.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: New Zealand Customs export declaration (electronic export entry filed through the New Zealand Customs Service Trade Single Window and cleared for departure)
Bill of Lading, Master Air Waybill, or House Air Waybill showing the New Zealand port or airport of departure and the overseas destination
Commercial invoice and contract of sale with the overseas buyer, clearly identifying the goods or services, the incoterm, and the 0% GST treatment
Proof of physical export, including container tracking, customs departure confirmation, or departure report evidencing that the goods left New Zealand

Foreign exchange and inward remittance evidence, including SWIFT MT103, bank remittance advice, foreign exchange contract, or, where required, a bank-issued Inward Remittance Certificate (FIRC) or equivalent New Zealand inward remittance certificate proving export proceeds were received from the foreign buyer
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: Inland Revenue can audit export zero-rating through review of GST returns, invoicing, customs records, shipping documents, and bank remittance evidence. If an export zero-rating is unsupported, incorrectly claimed, or later discovered to involve false or misleading documentation, the supply is recharacterised as taxable at 15% GST, with use-of-money interest running from the original return due date and retrospective clawback of any resulting refund. Shortfall penalties under the Tax Administration Act 1994 apply: 20% for an unacceptable tax position, 40% for failure to disclose a tax position, 100% for an abusive tax position, and 150% for evasion or fraudulent activity. Criminal prosecution is possible for knowingly providing false information or creating false documents to support a zero-rated export claim. The taxpayer bears the burden of proving the export documentation requirements, and all supporting records must generally be retained for at least seven years.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Te Pūtea Matua)
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: New Zealand operates under a free-float exchange rate regime and maintains no comprehensive foreign exchange control legislation. The Reserve Bank of New Zealand does not require prior approval for typical current-account or capital-account transactions, and the New Zealand dollar is fully convertible without mandatory surrender requirements. Exports may retain receipts in foreign currency indefinitely, and no conversion ratio is imposed by statute. Profit remittance, dividend distribution, and loan repayments are freely permitted subject to standard tax withholding and corporate documentation requirements. Non-resident ownership of the New Zealand limited company is allowed, and the business scope of a no-code website builder does not trigger sector-specific FDI screening. The practical constraints are therefore not FX controls but banking due diligence, because banks must independently verify beneficial ownership, source of funds, and legitimate business purpose. The Reserve Bank focuses on prudential supervision and systemic stability, leaving transaction-level currency freedom to market participants. For a standard SaaS entity, no special central bank license or exchange approval is required for treasury operations.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: No statutory surrender rules apply in New Zealand. Exporters and digital service providers may retain all foreign currency earnings offshore or in local foreign currency accounts, with no mandatory conversion timeline and no required percentage sale of export proceeds to the local market.

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Offshore fintech electronic money institutions are not legally barred from supporting New Zealand entities, but they are not a primary treasury rail. New Zealand does not issue UK-style EMI licences, and most foreign EMIs must partner with a licensed local bank or rely on a transactional banking wrapper to obtain a NZD settlement capability. For a corporate exporter with cross-border SaaS billing, an offshore EMI can serve as a secondary collection and disbursement channel, particularly for multi-currency payouts and low-fee trade settlements. However, the onboarding viability as a main operating account is Medium-to-Low because of reputational risk, the absence of full NZ banking licence protections, limited capital verification capacity, and the requirement to maintain a domestic bank relationship for statutory and liquidity purposes. The prudent treasury structure is to keep the primary NZD operational account at a Tier-1 bank and use a regulated international EMI only for ancillary billing streams such as Stripe/Billing or Paddle settlements.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: Statutory directors of a New Zealand limited company are not generally required to appear physically in-branch for account opening. Most Tier-1 banks permit remote onboarding using electronically verified identification, video interviews, and notarised or apostilled corporate documents. A non-resident director can typically complete due diligence via secure video conference and digital ID verification, supplemented by certified copies of passport, proof of address, and company constitution. Some banks may request an in-country authorised representative or a physical service address for correspondence, but full consular proxy opening is not a standard alternative. Where the bank considers the entity higher risk due to cross-border ownership, it may impose an enhanced interview requirement at its commercial discretion.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Beneficial ownership obscured by offshore trust or nominee shareholder layers above the New Zealand operating company.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Certified trust deed and current trust register; written UBO declaration identifying all direct and indirect controlling persons; notarised passports and proof of residence for settlor, protector, and beneficiaries; independent legal opinion confirming the trust's economic substance; source-of-wealth and source-of-funds statements covering the trust and ultimate controllers.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: The no-code website builder business model receives high-volume digital payments from unidentified end users, creating potential third-party money-laundering exposure through the platform.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Detailed product portfolio showing the actual low-code software and template functionality; privacy policy and terms of service; data-flow diagram and payment-flow architecture; SOC 2 Type II audit report; customer onboarding and transaction monitoring procedures; evidence of country-level IP blocking and sanctions screening logs; and an enterprise customer due diligence policy for B2B subscribers.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: The initial capital injection or intercompany funding has an unusual or non-transparent source that does not match projected working capital needs.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Signed intercompany loan agreement or equity subscription agreement; audited financial statements of the funding entity; treasury board resolutions; full bank-statement trail from originating account through the New Zealand receiving account; declaration of source of funds; and tax filings or clearance certificates from the relevant revenue authorities.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Cross-border software sales create sanctions, export-control, or geopolitical risk because end users may be located in restricted jurisdictions.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Automated sanctions screening log covering all end users for the last 12 months; compliance manual explaining customer categorisation and prohibited jurisdiction policy; GeoIP restriction configuration evidence; OFAC/EU/UN sanctions screening integration results; sample trade-party screening reports; and a structured escalation protocol for blocked transactions.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Inbound capital injections should be routed via SWIFT MT103 or MT202 into a dedicated capital escrow or operational account at the chosen Tier-1 bank. The payment instruction must include the correct remittance currency, entity legal name, unique corporate registration number and the relevant purpose code for foreign investment or equity capital. For the no-code software builder, the inbound funds are likely intercompany loans or paid-up capital from shareholders; the bank will require a board resolution, a funds-receipt declaration, and a source-of-funds statement. There is no central bank conversion approval needed, but the injecting entity must ensure that all taxes, including non-resident withholding on interest or dividends, are addressed. Capital verification should be evidenced by the bank receipt, a chartered accountant's statement, and updated shareholder register entries showing the issued share allocation.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Outbound trade and operational disbursements should be executed over SWIFT MT103 for regular supplier and licensing payments, commercial letters of credit for high-value or documentary trade, and documentary collections for lower-risk, document-driven settlements. The treasury should maintain a New Zealand-dollar operating account plus a multi-currency clearing capability for SaaS subscription inflows and outbound contractor payments. Payment rails such as Stripe and Paddle may be used for retail billing, but corporate-to-corporate settlements should flow through the licensed bank channels to maintain auditability and reduce clearing disruption.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Plain-vanilla deliverable foreign exchange forwards with registered New Zealand banks
Non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) only in jurisdictions where deliverable hedging is impractical or when required by a counterparty's local regulations
Cross-currency swaps for long-term NZD/USD balance-sheet hedging on intercompany loans
Foreign-currency accounts maintained at domestic banks as a natural structural hedge
Forward rate agreements limited to transparent underlying commercial exposures

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual Return (Form AR) under the Companies Act 1993, confirming directors, registered office, share structure, and compliance standing
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Registrar of Companies, New Zealand Companies Office, Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 20 working days after the annual return date, being the anniversary of the company's date of registration
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Failure to deliver the annual return may trigger the Registrar's notice of intention to remove the company from the New Zealand Register under section 318 of the Companies Act 1993. Continued non-compliance for a further period can result in administrative strike-off without liability, court-ordered restoration fees, director offence liability, and fines of up to NZD 10,000.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual Corporate Income Tax Return (IR4) and associated tax reconciliation for the New Zealand company
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Inland Revenue Department (Te Tari Taake), New Zealand
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: For a standard balance date of 31 March, the IR4 must be filed no later than 30 September; for an approved non-standard balance date, filing is due within 6 months after the end of the balance date, subject to any IRD tax-agent extension arrangement
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late filing penalties apply, including an initial NZD 50 penalty for each late return and escalating penalties for subsequent failures. The Commissioner may issue default assessments, impose shortfall penalties of up to 20% of the tax position, apply use-of-money interest on unpaid tax, and instigate criminal proceedings for persistent non-compliance.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Audited statutory financial statements and the signed audit report, but only if the company is not exempt by reason of being a small, non-FMC, non-overseas-owned entity
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: New Zealand Companies Office or Financial Markets Authority, depending on the reporting classification; filed with the Registrar where the Financial Reporting Act 2013 applicable
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: No later than the due date for the corresponding annual return period; for a company with a 31 March balance date, this is generally 30 September. FMC reporting entities may have an shorter filing period under the Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: A company that is required to prepare audited financial statements but fails to do so is in breach of the Financial Reporting Act 2013 and the Companies Act 1993. The Registrar may require the financial statements to be filed, may take enforcement action, and directors may be liable for fines of up to NZD 10,000 for continued non-compliance.

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: A statutory audit is mandatory if the company is an FMC reporting entity under the Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013; is an overseas-owned company; or does not qualify as a small company under the Financial Reporting Act 2013. A company is non-small and therefore loses the small-company audit exemption if at either of the last two consecutive balance dates it had total assets equal to or exceeding NZD 5,000,000, total revenue equal to or exceeding NZD 10,000,000, or 50 or more full-time equivalent employees. In addition, an audit must always be appointed if shareholders holding at least 5% of the voting rights validly require one, or if a court so orders. A small company may avoid appointing an auditor only by a unanimous shareholder resolution and filing the prescribed audit-exemption notice with the Registrar.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: Financial statements must be prepared in accordance with generally accepted accounting practice in New Zealand as established by the External Reporting Board. Tier 1 entities must apply full New Zealand equivalents to IFRS (NZ IFRS). Tier 2 entities without public accountability may apply NZ IFRS with reduced disclosure regimes (NZ IFRS RDR). A small company preparing financial statements strictly for internal shareholder purposes is not required to comply with full NZ IFRS unless the financial statements are lodged with a regulator, but once a statutory audit threshold is triggered, the financial statements must comply with the applicable XRB accounting standards.

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: New Zealand does not maintain a separate annual UBO filing docket for a standard domestic limited company. The annual return to the Companies Office confirms the registered office, directors, and issued shareholding as at the annual return date. Any change of directors, allotment of shares, transfer of shares, or change of registered office must be filed with the Registrar within 20 working days of the relevant event. The company must maintain a contemporaneous internal ownership and control record, including ultimate beneficial ownership details, and must produce it to the Registrar or IRD when requested. The 30-day reporting window is not applicable to a New Zealand company; the correct statutory event reporting window is 20 working days.
mandatory_on_site_statutory_registers: Register of Charges and Mortgages, if any security has been created
Minute Book containing minutes of directors' meetings and shareholders' meetings
Accounting records and corporate records retained for at least seven years

recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.registered_office_or_agent_market_range_: USD 250 - USD 850 per annum for a New Zealand registered office and registered agent service, depending on provider and compliance package
recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.statutory_audit_estimated_fee_usd: USD 4,000 - USD 15,000 per annum for a typical non-exempt New Zealand limited company, subject to transaction volume, subsidiary structure, and accounting complexity

corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: New Zealand imposes a single flat 28% corporate income tax rate on all NZ-resident companies, with no separate free-zone holiday, patent box, or preferential export regime; the principal effective-rate relief is the refundable R&D Tax Incentive of 15% of eligible R&D expenditure, combined with the imputation credit system that prevents double taxation on dividend distributions to NZ-resident shareholders; certain small-business depreciation, low-value asset, and software-development deductions may further reduce effective tax.
corporate_income_tax_regime.tax_loss_carryforward_limit_years: Unlimited (subject to the 49% shareholder continuity test or the same-or-similar business test; breach of continuity forgoes the loss carryforward)

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: IR4 – New Zealand Company Income Tax Return, e-filed through Inland Revenue myIR portal (www.ird.govt.nz) using the company IRD number; related-party international transactions are also reported in supplementary schedules and, where a transfer-pricing disclosure is required, through the associated International Questionnaire / TP schedules (IR4J / IR4S variants) maintained by Inland Revenue.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.reporting_frequency: Annual (one IR4 per income year; provisional tax is paid in three instalments during the year, but no separate quarterly corporate income tax return is filed).
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: For a standard 31 March balance date, the IR4 must be filed by 7 July of the immediately following income year; for non-standard balance dates, the filing deadline is the 7th day of the 4th month after balance date, subject to tax agent extension arrangements; terminal tax is generally payable by 7 February or 7 April depending on provisional tax arrangements, and use-of-money interest applies from the due date.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Total gross income from all New Zealand and foreign sources for the income year, before deduction of expenses.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: For this NZ no-code website builder entity, include all SaaS subscription fees, low-code platform licence fees, visual website template sales, Stripe_Billing and Paddle settlements, and any performance-based or reseller revenue attributable to the NZ entity. Recognise revenue in NZD at the applicable exchange rate. Do not deduct payment-processor fees in this box; those are entered as operating expenses. For non-resident-controlled companies, any amount diverted to an offshore related entity without a valid arm’s-length service or royalty arrangement must be brought back into gross income for NZ tax purposes.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Allowable business deductions: software development, hosting, cloud infrastructure, subcontractors, marketing, customer support, payment gateway fees, salaries, regulatory licences, and other ordinary expenses.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Only expenses incurred in deriving assessable income are deductible. Intercompany charges for offshore coding, IP licensing, management fees, or shared services must satisfy the arm's-length standard and must be supported by contemporaneous transfer-pricing documentation. Amounts paid as royalties, interest, or fees to non-residents may trigger non-resident withholding tax (NRWT) obligations; if the deduction is based on a sham invoice from a tax-haven parent, the deduction will be denied and penalties imposed.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Net taxable income or net taxable loss after deducting allowable expenses and offsetting carried-forward losses.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: The NZ-resident company is taxed on worldwide income at 28% irrespective of non-resident ownership. Loss carryforwards may be utilised only if the 49% shareholder continuity requirement is still met at the end of the income year; a change in foreign ownership of the NZ Ltd, or an issue of shares to a new offshore investor, may permanently forfeit the loss balance. Any loss offset claim must be supported by an ownership continuity schedule.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Income tax calculation on net taxable income at the corporate tax rate, before credits.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: The NZ tax on net taxable income is computed at 28%. There is no reduced corporate rate for non-resident shareholders or for export-oriented software sales. If a foreign parent operates through a New Zealand branch rather than an NZ subsidiary, the branch may be subject to a separate non-resident company return and final withholding on branch profits; here, because the payer is an NZ-incorporated limited company, the entity-level tax regime applies and the 28% rate is final at the company level until dividends are distributed.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Tax credits: resident withholding tax (RWT) credits on interest and dividends, imputation credits, foreign income tax credits, and the R&D tax incentive credit.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: The R&D tax incentive credit is calculated on eligible R&D expenditure using the 15% credit rate and may be refundable. Foreign income tax credits are available only where the same foreign income is also included in NZ taxable income; you must complete the applicable foreign tax credit schedule. Imputation credits received from other NZ companies may reduce NZ tax payable, but imputation credits cannot be refunded to non-resident shareholders and cannot be used to satisfy NRWT in respect of dividends paid overseas.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Tax payable or refund due, net of all credits and instalments.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: The company must settle any terminal tax balance by the statutory due date. A refund arising from the refundable R&D credit or excessive provisional tax may be paid by Inland Revenue, but Inland Revenue first applies the refund against any outstanding tax, late-filing penalties, or director-held tax debts. For a non-resident-owned NZ Ltd, any later dividend distribution out of post-tax retained earnings will be subject to separate NRWT at the time of distribution; simply overpaying company tax does not discharge the shareholder-level NRWT.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Related-party international transactions, transfer-pricing method, and controlled transactions with non-resident associates.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Disclose all material related-party transactions: licence fees to the foreign parent for the no-code platform IP, intercompany loans, management charges, technical services, and revenue share with offshore sales agents. State the transfer-pricing method applied (CUP, Resale Price, Cost Plus, TNMM, or Profit Split) and identify the tested party. If the NZ entity is merely a contract manufacturer or distributor of digital templates with little functional substance, Inland Revenue may reallocate profits under the arm’s-length principle. Keep the Local File, Master File, and OECD-aligned TP analysis ready for inspection; CbC reporting obligations apply to MNE groups with consolidated revenue above NZD 1.13 billion.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Director declaration and certification that the return is true and correct in all material respects.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: This is a personally signed electronic certification. A director who signs an IR4 knowing that revenue from foreign subscribers was omitted, that offshore related-party invoices are fictitious, or that transfer prices were manipulated to strip profit out of New Zealand, is exposed to civil shortfall penalties and criminal prosecution for evasion under section 143A of the Tax Administration Act 1994. Non-resident directors are not insulated by their foreign residence; New Zealand criminal and enforcement jurisdiction extends to them for revenue attributable to an NZ company, and departure prohibition orders can prevent them from leaving New Zealand while tax debts or investigations are outstanding.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late filing of the IR4 triggers a late filing penalty (for companies, the initial statutory late-filing penalty is NZ$250, with incremental late-payment penalties where tax remains unpaid); unpaid tax accrues use-of-money interest at the prescribed rate, plus a 1% late-payment penalty on the day after the due date, a further 4% after seven days, and an ongoing 1% per month for continual default. Civil shortfall penalties range from 20% for not taking reasonable care or taking an unacceptable tax position, to 100% for an abusive tax position, and 150% for evasion or a similar act. Criminal prosecution may apply where a false return is filed with intent to evade tax, with fines of up to NZ$50,000 and imprisonment of up to 5 years for individuals; there is no minimum monetary threshold for criminal fraud — the triggering criterion is fraudulent conduct and deliberate concealment.

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: 30% NRWT on gross dividends paid by an NZ-resident company to a non-resident shareholder, although a lower DTA rate may apply (typically 15% for portfolio dividends and 5% or 0% for substantial corporate shareholdings depending on the applicable double tax agreement); imputation credits do not reduce the gross dividend subject to NRWT but are relevant to the domestic tax integration system.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: To invoke DTA relief, the non-resident shareholder must obtain a valid Tax Residency Certificate (TRC) from its home jurisdiction and deliver it to the NZ payer before the payment date, together with a beneficial-ownership declaration confirming that the recipient is the true owner of the dividend and is not a conduit or fiscally transparent nominee. The NZ payer must document the treaty country, the applicable DTA article, the ownership percentage (for the reduced 5% direct-dividend rate), and confirmation that the recipient has no New Zealand permanent establishment to which the dividend is effectively connected. The declaration should be made on the appropriate Inland Revenue non-resident withholding tax forms (or equivalent TRC/IR3NR certification); if treaty relief was not applied at source, the non-resident may claim a refund from Inland Revenue or invoke the Mutual Agreement Procedure under the DTA.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: Domestic NRWT is 15% on interest and 15% on royalties paid to non-residents; DTA rates commonly reduce interest to 10% or 0% for qualifying financial institutions and royalties to 10% (for example, under many of New Zealand’s comprehensive DTAs), provided the recipient is the beneficial owner and meets the limitation-of-benefits conditions; New Zealand’s Approved Issuer Levy regime permits a 2% levy to be paid by an approved issuer in lieu of NRWT on certain interest payments to foreign lenders, subject to strict conditions; intercompany royalties for the use of software IP, trademarks, platform technology, and know-how paid by the NZ no-code builder to a foreign related party are fully chargeable to NRWT unless an applicable treaty reduces the rate.

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: New Zealand does not prescribe a single statutory de-minimis threshold for all related-party transactions; however, Inland Revenue’s transfer-pricing compliance framework requires contemporaneous documentation for material cross-border related-party transactions and expects a Local File/Master File structure for significant MNE operations; CbCR is mandatory for groups with consolidated revenue of at least NZD 1.13 billion; in practice, related-party transactions above approximately NZD 10 million annual value are treated as material, but the absence of any threshold does not eliminate the obligation to maintain arm’s-length pricing evidence and IRD records under Tax Administration Act 1994.
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: New Zealand does not operate a Caribbean/BVI-style Economic Substance Regulations statute, but economic substance is embedded in the corporate residency rules, permanent establishment thresholds, transfer-pricing principles, the general anti-avoidance rule in sections BG1/GA1 of the Income Tax Act 2007, and anti-sham doctrine. For a no-code website builder and low-code platform provider, the Core Income-Generating Activities — product development, contract execution, user data control, pricing, risk management, and revenue settlement — must be performed by employees and assets physically located in New Zealand for the NZ company to be regarded as the true beneficial owner of the income. If the foreign parent or a Singapore/Hong Kong/BVI affiliate performs the CIGA while the NZ entity merely invoices subscribers, Inland Revenue can re-allocate profits to the entity where the economically significant people and functions are located, or deny treaty benefits on the ground that the NZ entity is a shell without real business purpose.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Tax Evasion / Fraudulent Omission of Foreign Digital Revenue
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: The director of the NZ no-code website builder intentionally omits non-resident subscriber revenue received through Stripe_Billing and Paddle, instructs payment processors to divert revenue into a foreign bank account, issues false invoices for fake marketing services, or submits an IR4 knowingly understating taxable income in order to avoid 28% corporate tax.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Tax Administration Act 1994 sections 141A and 143A: civil shortfall penalty of 150% of the evaded tax, plus use-of-money interest; criminal liability for evasion by a company officer or director includes a fine up to NZ$50,000 and/or imprisonment for up to 5 years for each offence; the Commissioner may also issue a default assessment based on best information, and the tax debt becomes immediately recoverable.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: The corporate veil is pierced for fraud and evasion: a director who knowingly concealed revenue is personally liable for the resulting tax shortfall and penalties under the director-liability provisions in the Tax Administration Act 1994; the court may order restitution of company assets under section 301 of the Companies Act 1993; Inland Revenue may seek a departure prohibition order under section 157 of the TAA, effectively blacklisting the director from air travel until the tax debt is secured; conviction can also lead to director disqualification and overseas asset tracing with enforcement through mutual assistance treaties.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Transfer Pricing Manipulation / Royalty Stripping to an Offshore IP Owner
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: The NZ Ltd pays an excessive deductible royalty or licence fee to a Hong Kong/Singapore/BVI parent for the no-code software IP, charges below arm's-length prices to the offshore sales affiliate, or signs intra-group service agreements with no performed functions, while the actual economic substance of the platform invention, development responsibility, user-interface ownership, and risk-bearing remains in New Zealand; the result is a systematic transfer of taxable profit to a low-tax jurisdiction.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Income Tax Act 2007 section GC13 empowers the Commissioner of Inland Revenue to impute an arm's-length price and adjust the NZ company’s taxable income; the corresponding shortfall penalty under Tax Administration Act 1994 for an unacceptable tax position or abusive transfer-pricing position can reach 20% to 100%, with a dedicated transfer-pricing shortfall penalty of 40% on the quantum of adjustment in serious cases; use-of-money interest runs from the original due date.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: A director who signs transfer-pricing documentation or supports board minutes falsely describing non-existent functions, assets, or risks may be found to have been involved in misleading tax conduct; liability can attach personally for the unpaid tax adjustment if the company is insolvent; the court may order recovery of artificially extracted royalties from the director as transaction-concealment or sham compensation under the Companies Act 1993; travel restrictions and prosecution for false statements are available, and egregious conduct can result in criminal imprisonment of up to 5 years.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Sham Shell Company / Abusive Treaty and Economic-Substance Avoidance
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: The NZ no-code website builder is structured as an incorporated shell with no physical office, no local employees, no independent bank control, and no real management functions in New Zealand; all substantive CIGA are delegated to a foreign affiliate, while the company is used only to sign contracts, invoice subscribers, access New Zealand’s DTA network, and route profits through subsidies/fees/royalties to a tax-haven service provider; the company has no effective economic reality and exists solely to obtain treaty withholding-tax reductions or to create the appearance of high-credibility New Zealand origin for the software products.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The general anti-avoidance rule in sections BG1 and GA1 of the Income Tax Act 2007 permits Inland Revenue to reconstruct the arrangement and tax the economic substance; the company may be treated as non-resident or as having a permanent establishment elsewhere, thereby denying treaty benefits and making all New Zealand-source fees subject to NRWT at the statutory rate; the abusive tax position penalty is 100% of the shortfall, with 150% penalty and criminal prosecution available if the shell structure is used with intent to evade tax; false declarations made to payment processors or tax authorities also constitute criminal fraud under section 143A.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Where a company is a mere facade or sham, New Zealand courts will pierce the corporate veil and hold the directing mind and hands personally liable for the tax owed; directors are exposed to civil asset restitution, recovery actions and compensation orders under section 301 of the Companies Act 1993 for knowingly participating in concealed transactions, and can be disqualified under section 383; Insolvency officers may recover fees paid through the shell as voidable transactions; Inland Revenue can use section 157 departure prohibition orders to blacklist a director from leaving New Zealand until outstanding assessments are satisfied, and fraudulent misuse of a corporate facade carries criminal liability including imprisonment for up to 5 years in addition to personal seizure of proceeds of crime.
